Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Rohan's eyes still glaze over when he recounts the day a Category 5 typhoon ravaged his hometown in the Philippines. He was just 19 then, home from college for summer break. The howling winds and lashing rains were so intense that they seemed to shred the air itself. His family huddled together in their small house as it shuddered and groaned, threatening to collapse at any moment. Rohan's mother clutched him tightly, her face etched with fear, as his father tried to secure the doors against the storm surge. As the storm raged on, a massive tree branch crashed through the roof, barely missing them. The impact sent shards of wood and debris flying everywhere, leaving Rohan dazed and disoriented. When he stumbled out into the devastated streets later that day, the sights and smells overwhelmed him - uprooted trees, destroyed homes, the stench of mud and saltwater. He remembers feeling like he was walking through a war zone. It's been three years since then, but Rohan still experiences the aftermath in visceral ways. When his neck throbs with pain, as it often does after long hours hunched over his laptop designing user interfaces, he feels a familiar dread creeping up on him. He becomes convinced that something is seriously wrong with his health - a tumor, a blood clot - and that this time, there's no escape. The fear of being physically unwell can become all-consuming, leading Rohan to trawl the internet for hours, researching possible causes and treatments. Sometimes, when he least expects it, the memories come flooding back in vivid detail. He'll catch a whiff of saltwater or damp earth, and suddenly he's reliving that terrible day - the screams, the crashing sounds, his family's desperate clinging to each other. The taste of mud and sweat fills his mouth once more, transporting him to a place where time seems to warp and bend. But there are moments when Rohan is consumed by intense emotions without any clear image or memory attached to them. He'll feel a suffocating grief or a creeping sense of unease that leaves him breathless and disoriented. In those times, he's at a loss to explain what's happening inside his head. Rohan has also begun to question the trustworthiness of others. Colleagues and friends try to reassure him with their words and smiles, but he can't shake off the feeling that they're all hiding something - just like the typhoon hid its fury behind an innocuous summer sky. He starts to wonder if anyone truly understands what it means to have lived through such a catastrophe. The sense of isolation has grown over time, leaving Rohan with the conviction that he no longer belongs anywhere. His design job is going well enough, but every social gathering feels forced, and online communities seem shallow compared to the depth of his own experiences. When asked about his future plans or goals, Rohan struggles to articulate anything beyond a hazy notion of "getting through each day." The once-vibrant colors of his world have dulled, as if seen through a gray filter. Lately, Rohan's begun to notice that he can no longer enjoy the simple pleasures in life without being yanked back into the vortex of memories. A stroll along the beach with friends turns into an exercise in vigilance - monitoring the horizon for signs of another storm brewing. His sleep has become fitful and fragmented, as if his mind is perpetually waiting for the next "attack." The realization that he can no longer keep going like this finally pushed Rohan to seek help. He hopes to find a way out of this living nightmare, to quiet the perpetual alarm bells in his head, and maybe - just maybe - begin to rediscover the colors and textures of life.
